clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive disorder caused by ABCB7 variants; ABCB7 is a mitochondrial inner-membrane ATP-binding cassette transporter required for cytosolic iron-sulphur cluster maturation.
Defined by the combination of early-onset, non-progressive or only slowly progressive spinocerebellar ataxia with a mild sideroblastic anaemia.
The ataxia usually dominates the clinical picture, presenting in infancy or early childhood with incoordination, gait disturbance and dysarthria.
The anaemia is typically mild and hypochromic and microcytic, often detected only on investigation, with ring sideroblasts on bone marrow examination.
Free erythrocyte protoporphyrin is characteristically raised, which helps distinguish it from ALAS2-related X-linked sideroblastic anaemia.
Almost exclusively affects males; obligate female carriers are usually asymptomatic but may show a minor dimorphic red-cell population.
Brain imaging may demonstrate cerebellar atrophy or hypoplasia.
Iron supplementation is unhelpful and risks iron overload, and the anaemia rarely requires transfusion.
reference.pathophysiology: ABCB7 on chromosome Xq13.3 encodes a half-type ATP-binding cassette transporter located in the inner mitochondrial membrane that exports a sulphur-containing intermediate needed for the biogenesis of cytosolic and nuclear iron-sulphur (Fe-S) clusters. Missense variants that partially impair this transporter disrupt cytosolic Fe-S cluster assembly and derange mitochondrial iron handling, so iron accumulates within perinuclear mitochondria of erythroid precursors to produce ring sideroblasts and a sideroblastic anaemia, while impaired Fe-S-dependent processes in the developing and mature nervous system, particularly the cerebellum, give rise to the characteristic ataxia. Because the gene lies on the X chromosome and the variants are typically hypomorphic rather than null, the disease manifests in hemizygous males with a comparatively mild, largely non-progressive course, whereas heterozygous females are protected by the wild-type allele.
additionalDifferentials: ALAS2-related X-linked sideroblastic anaemia, which lacks ataxia
Other congenital sideroblastic anaemias (for example SLC25A38 and GLRX5 related)
Myopathy, lactic acidosis and sideroblastic anaemia (MLASA; PUS1, YARS2)
Friedreich ataxia and other early-onset hereditary ataxias
Ataxia with isolated vitamin E deficiency and abetalipoproteinaemia
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film (hypochromic microcytic, sometimes dimorphic)
Bone marrow examination with Perls' Prussian-blue stain for ring sideroblasts
Iron studies including ferritin, with vigilance for iron overload
Brain MRI for cerebellar atrophy or hypoplasia
Molecular genetic testing of ABCB7 with exclusion of ALAS2
Structured neurological assessment of the ataxia
redFlags: Evidence of iron overload, especially after inappropriate iron therapy or transfusion
Developmental regression rather than the expected static course
reference.prognosis: The ataxia is typically non-progressive or only slowly progressive and the anaemia is mild, so most affected males have a near-normal life expectancy provided iron overload is avoided.
pitfalls: The anaemia can be so mild that it is overlooked, and the ataxia is then wrongly attributed to another cause.
Iron supplementation is inappropriate and risks iron overload.
The condition is easily confused with Friedreich ataxia and other early-onset ataxias.
Only males are typically affected, so a negative family history among female relatives is unhelpful.
references: Reviews of the congenital sideroblastic anaemias
